_link.title: I can define and apply the concept of context-specific effectiveness

toLevel2.stem: What does 'context-specific effectiveness' mean in relation to coping with stress?

options.text: Selecting a coping strategy appropriate for the unique demands of the stressor
options.feedback: Correct. Context-specific effectiveness involves choosing a strategy suited to the specific demands, circumstances, resources, environment, and timing of the stressor.

options.text: Using the same coping strategy for every stressful situation
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness means the strategy should match the unique demands of each situation, not using the same strategy every time.

options.text: Choosing a coping strategy based on what is easiest to do
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness is about choosing what is most appropriate for the situation, not what is easiest.

options.text: Avoiding all coping strategies to let stress resolve naturally
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness involves actively selecting an appropriate strategy, not avoiding coping altogether.

toLevel2.stem: Which of the following factors should be considered when determining if a coping strategy is context-specifically effective?

options.text: Individual circumstances, available resources, the environment, and timing
options.feedback: Correct. Context-specific effectiveness requires considering the person's circumstances, resources, environment, and timing when selecting a strategy.

options.text: Only the type of stressor and nothing else
options.feedback: Incorrect. While the stressor matters, context-specific effectiveness also considers circumstances, resources, environment, and timing.

options.text: Only the person's age and gender
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness considers a broader range of factors including circumstances, resources, environment, and timing.

options.text: Only whether the strategy has worked for other people
options.feedback: Incorrect. What works for others may not work in a different context. The strategy must match the individual's unique situation.

toLevel2.stem: Why is the same coping strategy not equally effective in all situations?

options.text: Because different situations have different demands, resources, and circumstances that require different approaches
options.feedback: Correct. Each stressful situation has unique demands, and what works in one context may not be appropriate in another.

options.text: Because all coping strategies are equally ineffective
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping strategies can be effective, but their effectiveness depends on whether they match the specific context.

options.text: Because people should never change their coping approach
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness requires adapting strategies to match the situation, which may mean changing approach.

options.text: Because only one coping strategy exists for all situations
options.feedback: Incorrect. Multiple coping strategies exist, and their effectiveness depends on the context in which they are used.

toLevel2.stem: A student who has not yet studied for an upcoming SAC creates a study timetable and seeks teacher help. What concept does this demonstrate?

options.text: Context-specific effectiveness, because the strategies match the demands of the situation
options.feedback: Correct. Creating a timetable and seeking help are appropriate for a student who needs to study, demonstrating context-specific effectiveness.

options.text: Poor coping, because these strategies are never effective
options.feedback: Incorrect. These strategies are effective for this context. Creating a study plan and seeking help directly address the demands of the situation.

options.text: Avoidance, because the student is avoiding the exam
options.feedback: Incorrect. Creating a timetable and seeking help are approach strategies that directly confront the stressor, not avoidance.

options.text: Random coping, because any strategy would have worked equally well
options.feedback: Incorrect. These strategies were selected because they match the context. Not all strategies would be equally effective here.

toLevel2.stem: For a student who has already studied thoroughly for a SAC, would creating a study timetable be equally context-specifically effective?

options.text: No, because the strategy is less appropriate when the student has already prepared
options.feedback: Correct. Context-specific effectiveness means the strategy should match the demands. A well-prepared student has different needs than one who has not yet studied.

options.text: Yes, because study timetables are always the best strategy
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness means no strategy is always the best. A timetable is less needed when the student is already prepared.

options.text: Yes, because context does not matter when choosing coping strategies
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context is central to context-specific effectiveness. The same strategy can be more or less appropriate depending on the situation.

options.text: No, because creating timetables is never a good coping strategy
options.feedback: Incorrect. Creating a timetable can be effective in the right context. It is less needed when the student has already studied, but it is not inherently a poor strategy.

toLevel2.stem: Context-specific effectiveness means the same coping strategy is equally effective in all situations.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness recognises that the same strategy is NOT equally effective in all situations. Effectiveness depends on the context.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Context-specific effectiveness means the appropriateness of a strategy depends on the specific demands, circumstances, resources, environment, and timing.

toLevel2.stem: When evaluating a coping strategy, individual circumstances, resources, environment, and timing should all be considered.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Context-specific effectiveness involves considering all of these factors when evaluating whether a coping strategy is appropriate.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Incorrect. All of these factors — circumstances, resources, environment, and timing — are important for determining context-specific effectiveness.

toLevel2.stem: Context-specific effectiveness refers to selecting a coping strategy that is {{blank:1}} for the unique {{blank:2}} of the stressor.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness is about selecting the most appropriate strategy, not the easiest one.
Incorrect. The strategy should be appropriate for the demands of the situation, not chosen based on cost.
Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness involves matching the strategy to the demands of the stressor, not its benefits.
Incorrect. The strategy should match the demands of the stressor, not focus on rewards.

toLevel2.stem: The same coping strategy is not equally effective in all {{blank:1}} or for all {{blank:2}}.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. While cultural factors may play a role, the key idea is that effectiveness varies across situations, not just countries.
Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness relates to the unique demands of different situations, not different seasons.
Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness is about different people having different needs, not animals.
Incorrect. The concept refers to different people, as individual circumstances and resources vary.

toLevel2.stem: When evaluating context-specific effectiveness, factors to consider include individual {{blank:1}}, available resources, the environment, and {{blank:2}}.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness considers individual circumstances, not physical attributes like height.
Incorrect. The relevant factor is individual circumstances, not appearance.
Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness considers timing as a factor, not luck.
Incorrect. The factors include timing, not popularity.

toLevel3.stem: Why do exam questions about coping strategies frequently ask students to evaluate context-specific effectiveness in a given scenario?

options.text: Because it tests whether students can analyse the specific details of a situation rather than making general claims about strategies
options.feedback: Correct. Evaluating context-specific effectiveness requires analysing the unique details of a scenario, demonstrating deeper understanding than general statements.

options.text: Because all exam questions are about the same topic every year
options.feedback: Incorrect. Exam questions vary, but they often test context-specific effectiveness because it requires analytical thinking about specific scenarios.

options.text: Because students should memorise which strategy is best for every possible situation
options.feedback: Incorrect. The point is to analyse each unique scenario, not memorise fixed answers for every situation.

options.text: Because examiners want students to choose the same strategy every time
options.feedback: Incorrect. Examiners want students to demonstrate that they can evaluate strategies based on context, not apply the same strategy every time.

toLevel3.stem: How does the concept of available resources relate to context-specific effectiveness?

options.text: A strategy that requires resources the person does not have cannot be context-specifically effective for them
options.feedback: Correct. If a person lacks the resources needed for a particular strategy, that strategy is not context-specifically effective for their situation.

options.text: Resources are irrelevant because all strategies can be used without any resources
options.feedback: Incorrect. Many strategies require specific resources. A strategy requiring unavailable resources is not context-specifically effective.

options.text: Having more resources always means better coping regardless of strategy choice
options.feedback: Incorrect. Even with many resources, the strategy must still match the demands of the situation to be context-specifically effective.

options.text: Resources only refer to financial wealth and nothing else
options.feedback: Incorrect. Resources include time, knowledge, social support, and other factors, not just financial wealth.

toLevel3.stem: A student facing a family conflict uses a study timetable as their coping strategy. Is this context-specifically effective?

options.text: No, because a study timetable does not address the demands of a family conflict
options.feedback: Correct. A study timetable is designed for academic stressors, not family conflicts. Context-specific effectiveness requires matching the strategy to the demands of the situation.

options.text: Yes, because study timetables are always the best coping strategy
options.feedback: Incorrect. A study timetable is appropriate for academic stress but does not address the demands of a family conflict.

options.text: Yes, because any strategy that keeps you busy is effective for any stressor
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness requires the strategy to match the demands of the situation, not simply keep the person busy.

options.text: No, because study timetables are never effective for any situation
options.feedback: Incorrect. Study timetables can be effective for academic stressors. The issue is that they do not match the demands of a family conflict.

toLevel3.stem: How does timing affect the context-specific effectiveness of a coping strategy?

options.text: A strategy may be effective at one point in time but less effective at a different stage of the stressor
options.feedback: Correct. Timing matters because the demands of a stressor can change over time, making some strategies more or less appropriate at different points.

options.text: Timing has no effect on the effectiveness of coping strategies
options.feedback: Incorrect. Timing is one of the key factors in context-specific effectiveness. A strategy's appropriateness can change depending on when it is used.

options.text: Strategies should always be used at the same time regardless of the situation
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness recognises that timing affects when a strategy is most appropriate.

options.text: Only strategies used immediately after a stressor are ever effective
options.feedback: Incorrect. Different strategies may be effective at different times. The timing should match the current demands of the situation.

toLevel3.stem: Two students face the same exam. One has studied extensively and the other has not. Why might the same coping strategy be differently effective for each?

options.text: Their different circumstances mean they have different demands, making different strategies more appropriate for each
options.feedback: Correct. The prepared student and unprepared student have different needs, so the same strategy would not be equally appropriate for both.

options.text: Because the exam is inherently stressful for only one of them regardless of preparation
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both may experience stress, but their different preparation levels create different demands, affecting which strategies are context-specifically effective.

options.text: Because coping strategies never work for anyone in exam situations
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping strategies can be effective in exam situations when they match the specific demands of the individual's context.

options.text: Because the same strategy is always equally effective for everyone
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness means the same strategy can be more or less effective depending on individual circumstances.

toLevel3.stem: Which of the following best explains why general claims about coping strategies are insufficient for exam responses?

options.text: Because context-specific effectiveness requires analysis of the specific scenario details, not generic statements
options.feedback: Correct. Examiners want to see that students can evaluate strategies based on the specific demands, resources, and circumstances of the given scenario.

options.text: Because examiners do not know what coping strategies are
options.feedback: Incorrect. Examiners are well-informed. The issue is that general claims do not demonstrate the analytical skills needed to evaluate context-specific effectiveness.

options.text: Because there is only one correct coping strategy that applies to all situations
options.feedback: Incorrect. Multiple strategies exist and their effectiveness depends on context, which is why specific analysis is needed.

options.text: Because exam questions never mention specific scenarios
options.feedback: Incorrect. Exam questions frequently present specific scenarios and ask students to evaluate strategies in that context.

toLevel3.stem: A coping strategy that is effective in one situation is guaranteed to be effective in a different situation.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness means a strategy's appropriateness depends on the specific demands, resources, and circumstances of each situation.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The same strategy may not be effective in a different situation because the demands, resources, and circumstances may differ.

toLevel3.stem: Exam responses about coping should analyse the specific {{blank:1}} of the scenario rather than making {{blank:2}} claims about strategies.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Effective exam responses analyse the specific details of the scenario, not personal opinions.
Incorrect. While emotions may be part of the scenario, analysing the specific details of the situation is key for evaluating context-specific effectiveness.
Incorrect. The issue is that responses should avoid general claims. Specific analysis is what is needed.
Incorrect. Claims should be accurate, but they should also be specific to the scenario rather than general.

toLevel3.stem: A strategy requiring resources the person does not have is {{blank:1}} context-specifically effective because the strategy does not match their available {{blank:2}}.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. A strategy requiring unavailable resources is not context-specifically effective, because the person cannot implement it.
Incorrect. If the required resources are unavailable, the strategy cannot be effective regardless of other factors.
Incorrect. While time is one resource, the broader concept is available resources, which includes time, knowledge, support, and more.
Incorrect. The key factor here is available resources, not emotions.

toLevel3.stem: Context-specific effectiveness recognises that {{blank:1}} affects when a strategy is most appropriate, as the demands of a stressor can {{blank:2}} over time.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness considers timing, not luck, as a factor in strategy appropriateness.
Incorrect. While environment is a factor, timing specifically refers to when in the course of a stressor a strategy is applied.
Incorrect. Stressor demands can change over time, not necessarily disappear. The changing demands affect which strategies are most appropriate.
Incorrect. Stressor demands can change over time, which is why timing matters for context-specific effectiveness.

toLevel4.stem: Jess has just received bad news about a family member's health and is feeling overwhelmed with grief. Her friend suggests she should immediately start researching treatment options online. Apply context-specific effectiveness to evaluate this advice.

options.text: The advice may not be context-specifically effective because Jess is overwhelmed and may need emotional support first before she can engage in problem-solving
options.feedback: Correct. Given Jess's emotional state, she may need emotional support (addressing her grief) before she can effectively engage in researching treatment options. The timing and her current state affect which strategy is appropriate.

options.text: The advice is context-specifically effective because research is always the best response to bad news
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness depends on the individual's current state and needs. Jess is overwhelmed, so immediate problem-solving may not be appropriate.

options.text: The advice is ineffective because researching is never a useful coping strategy
options.feedback: Incorrect. Researching can be effective in the right context, but timing and the individual's emotional state matter. Right now, Jess may need emotional support first.

options.text: The advice is context-specifically effective because doing something is always better than doing nothing
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness is about doing the right thing for the situation, not just doing something. The strategy must match the current demands.

toLevel4.stem: Amir is stressed about a group project deadline tomorrow. He has not started his section and has no internet access at home tonight. His classmate suggests he research the topic online. Apply context-specific effectiveness to evaluate this suggestion.

options.text: The strategy is not context-specifically effective because Amir lacks the required resource (internet access) to implement it
options.feedback: Correct. Without internet access, Amir cannot carry out online research. Context-specific effectiveness requires that the strategy match the available resources.

options.text: The strategy is context-specifically effective because online research is always the best study method
options.feedback: Incorrect. Even if online research is useful generally, without internet access it cannot be implemented, making it inappropriate for this context.

options.text: The strategy is effective because Amir should get internet access before doing anything else
options.feedback: Incorrect. With a deadline tomorrow and no internet at home tonight, the more context-specifically effective approach would use available resources.

options.text: The strategy is not effective because group projects are never stressful
options.feedback: Incorrect. Group projects can be stressful. The issue is that the suggested strategy does not match Amir's available resources.

toLevel4.stem: A student has a SAC in three hours and feels extremely anxious. They consider two strategies: (A) creating a detailed study plan for the whole term, or (B) reviewing key notes for the most important topics. Which is more context-specifically effective and why?

options.text: Strategy B, because the timing requires a focused approach and there is not enough time for a detailed whole-term plan
options.feedback: Correct. With only three hours before the SAC, a focused review is more appropriate. A detailed whole-term plan does not match the timing demands of the situation.

options.text: Strategy A, because detailed planning is always the best approach to academic stress
options.feedback: Incorrect. While detailed planning can be effective, with only three hours before the SAC, it does not match the timing demands. Focused review is more appropriate.

options.text: Both strategies are equally effective regardless of the time available
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness means timing matters. With three hours, focused review is more appropriate than whole-term planning.

options.text: Neither strategy is effective because anxiety cannot be reduced
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both strategies could reduce anxiety in the right context, but Strategy B better matches the time constraint.

toLevel4.stem: Two friends both experience the loss of a pet. One copes by talking to family about their feelings, while the other copes by going for a run. Both report feeling better afterward. How does this relate to context-specific effectiveness?

options.text: Both strategies can be context-specifically effective because individual circumstances and preferences mean different people benefit from different approaches
options.feedback: Correct. Context-specific effectiveness recognises that individuals have different needs and resources, so different strategies can be appropriate for different people in similar situations.

options.text: Only talking about feelings is effective because it directly addresses the emotion
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness recognises that different strategies work for different people. Both friends felt better, suggesting both strategies matched their individual needs.

options.text: Only exercise is effective because it has physical health benefits
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both strategies were effective for their respective users. Context-specific effectiveness depends on the individual, not just the type of strategy.

options.text: Neither strategy is actually effective because pets cannot cause real stress
options.feedback: Incorrect. Loss of a pet can cause genuine stress. Both friends found effective strategies that matched their individual needs.

toLevel4.stem: A student experiencing chronic bullying at school is advised to 'just ignore it and distract yourself.' Evaluate this advice using context-specific effectiveness.

options.text: The advice may not be context-specifically effective because chronic bullying requires strategies that address the source of the stressor, not just distraction
options.feedback: Correct. Chronic bullying is an ongoing stressor that may require approach strategies such as seeking help from adults or authorities. Distraction alone does not address the source.

options.text: The advice is context-specifically effective because ignoring problems always works
options.feedback: Incorrect. Ignoring an ongoing stressor like chronic bullying does not address its source. Context-specific effectiveness may require more direct strategies.

options.text: The advice is effective because distraction is the only coping strategy that exists
options.feedback: Incorrect. Multiple coping strategies exist. For chronic bullying, strategies that address the source may be more context-specifically effective.

options.text: The advice is ineffective because no coping strategy can help with bullying
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping strategies can help with bullying, but they need to be context-specifically effective — addressing the source rather than just distraction.

toLevel4.stem: A teacher notices that a student's effective coping strategy for academic stress (making detailed study plans) is not helping them cope with social conflict. How does context-specific effectiveness explain this?

options.text: The demands of social conflict differ from academic stress, so a strategy effective for one is not necessarily effective for the other
options.feedback: Correct. Academic stress and social conflict have different demands. A study plan addresses academic demands but does not address the interpersonal nature of social conflict.

options.text: The student is using the wrong type of study plan for social conflict
options.feedback: Incorrect. Study plans are designed for academic demands. The issue is that social conflict has different demands that require different strategies.

options.text: A strategy that works for one stressor should always work for every stressor
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness means strategies must match the specific demands of each situation.

options.text: The teacher is wrong and the study plan is equally effective for both situations
options.feedback: Incorrect. Different stressors have different demands. A study plan does not address the demands of social conflict.

toLevel4.stem: A student in an exam writes: 'This coping strategy is effective because approach strategies always work.' Why would this response receive a low mark?

options.text: Because it makes a general claim rather than analysing the specific context to determine if the strategy matches the demands of the scenario
options.feedback: Correct. Context-specific effectiveness requires analysing specific details of the scenario. A general claim about approach strategies always working does not demonstrate this analysis.

options.text: Because approach strategies never work and the student is wrong
options.feedback: Incorrect. Approach strategies can be effective. The issue is the general claim rather than specific contextual analysis.

options.text: Because the response is too long for an exam answer
options.feedback: Incorrect. Length is not the issue. The response fails to analyse the specific context, which is what examiners are looking for.

options.text: Because examiners do not assess coping strategies in exams
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping strategies are assessed in VCE Psychology exams. The issue is the lack of context-specific analysis.

toLevel4.stem: When evaluating coping in an exam scenario, students should analyse the specific {{blank:1}} of the situation rather than stating that a particular strategy is {{blank:2}} effective.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. While background can be relevant, the key focus should be on the current demands of the situation.
Incorrect. While emotions are part of the scenario, analysing the demands helps determine if the strategy is context-specifically effective.
Incorrect. The problem is claiming a strategy is 'always' effective. Students should evaluate effectiveness based on the specific context.
Incorrect. While 'sometimes' is closer to being accurate, the key issue is that students should evaluate effectiveness based on the specific scenario details.

toLevel4.stem: Jess needs emotional {{blank:1}} before she can engage in problem-solving, showing that {{blank:2}} affects which strategy is most context-specifically effective.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. Jess needs emotional support (comfort and understanding), not emotional suppression.
Incorrect. Jess needs emotional support to address her grief, not emotional avoidance.
Incorrect. Timing, not luck, affects which strategy is most appropriate. Jess needs support first before she can problem-solve.
Incorrect. The factor demonstrated here is timing — Jess needs emotional support before she can engage in problem-solving.

toLevel4.stem: Amir's lack of {{blank:1}} access means online research is not context-specifically effective for him, demonstrating that available {{blank:2}} affect strategy appropriateness.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. The specific resource Amir lacks is internet access, which prevents him from doing online research.
Incorrect. The missing resource is internet access at home tonight, not school access.
Incorrect. The key factor is available resources, not grades. Without internet, the strategy cannot be implemented.
Incorrect. Available resources, not opinions, determine whether a strategy can be effectively implemented.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate the statement: 'There is one universally best coping strategy that is always context-specifically effective regardless of the situation.'

options.text: This contradicts the concept of context-specific effectiveness, which recognises that different situations require different strategies based on unique demands and circumstances
options.feedback: Correct. Context-specific effectiveness explicitly recognises that no single strategy is universally best. The appropriateness of a strategy depends on the specific context.

options.text: This is correct because science has identified one optimal coping strategy for all situations
options.feedback: Incorrect. No single strategy is optimal for all situations. Context-specific effectiveness requires matching strategies to specific demands.

options.text: This is correct because context does not affect coping effectiveness
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context is central to the concept of context-specific effectiveness. It directly affects which strategies are appropriate.

options.text: This is neither correct nor incorrect because coping strategies have no measurable effectiveness
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping effectiveness can be evaluated, and it depends on context. The statement contradicts context-specific effectiveness.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse how context-specific effectiveness challenges a 'one-size-fits-all' approach to stress management programs in schools.

options.text: Schools should offer diverse strategies because students face different stressors with different demands, resources, and circumstances that require different approaches
options.feedback: Correct. Context-specific effectiveness means a single program will not address every student's needs. Diverse strategies allow students to select approaches matching their unique circumstances.

options.text: Schools should teach only one strategy because simplicity is more effective
options.feedback: Incorrect. Teaching only one strategy ignores the principle that different contexts require different approaches.

options.text: Schools should not teach coping strategies because they are never effective
options.feedback: Incorrect. Coping strategies can be effective when context-specifically matched. Schools should teach diverse strategies for different situations.

options.text: Context-specific effectiveness supports a one-size-fits-all approach because all students face the same stressors
options.feedback: Incorrect. Students face different stressors with different demands. Context-specific effectiveness argues against a one-size-fits-all approach.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'If context-specific effectiveness means any strategy can be effective in some context, then all strategies are equally valuable.' Critically evaluate this reasoning.

options.text: This is flawed because context-specific effectiveness requires evaluating each strategy against the specific demands of the current situation, not assuming all are equally valuable
options.feedback: Correct. While many strategies can be effective in some context, in any given situation some strategies will be more appropriate than others. Strategies must be evaluated against specific demands.

options.text: This is correct because all strategies are equally effective in every situation
options.feedback: Incorrect. Strategies are not equally effective in every situation. Their effectiveness depends on how well they match the specific context.

options.text: This is correct because context-specific effectiveness means there are no bad strategies
options.feedback: Incorrect. Some strategies can be inappropriate for specific contexts. Context-specific effectiveness requires matching strategies to demands.

options.text: This is flawed only because some strategies never work in any context
options.feedback: Incorrect. The flaw is more nuanced — in any specific situation, strategies must be evaluated against the demands. The value of a strategy depends on the context.

toLevel5.stem: Compare the value of context-specific effectiveness as a concept for psychological practice versus for exam assessment. How does its value differ in these two applications?

options.text: In practice it guides clinicians to tailor interventions; in exams it requires students to demonstrate analytical thinking about specific scenarios rather than memorised generalisations
options.feedback: Correct. In practice, context-specific effectiveness guides personalised intervention. In exams, it requires scenario-specific analysis, testing deeper understanding.

options.text: It has value only in exams and no relevance to real-world psychological practice
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness is highly relevant to practice — clinicians must tailor strategies to individual clients and situations.

options.text: It has value only in practice and no relevance to exam assessment
options.feedback: Incorrect. It is a key assessed concept in VCE Psychology, requiring students to evaluate strategies in specific scenarios.

options.text: It has equal value in both and functions identically in practice and exams
options.feedback: Incorrect. While the concept is the same, its application differs — practice involves real-world tailoring, while exams test analytical ability.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate how the concept of context-specific effectiveness interacts with Lazarus and Folkman's transactional model of stress. How do these concepts complement each other?

options.text: L&F's secondary appraisal evaluates coping resources, and context-specific effectiveness determines whether the chosen strategy matches the situation — together they explain how people select and evaluate strategies
options.feedback: Correct. L&F's model explains the appraisal process, while context-specific effectiveness evaluates whether the chosen strategy is appropriate. Together they provide a complete picture of coping selection and evaluation.

options.text: They contradict each other because L&F says one strategy fits all
options.feedback: Incorrect. L&F's model recognises individual appraisals and coping resources, which aligns with context-specific effectiveness.

options.text: They are completely unrelated concepts with no connection
options.feedback: Incorrect. Both relate to how people select and evaluate coping strategies. L&F's secondary appraisal and context-specific effectiveness are complementary.

options.text: Context-specific effectiveness replaces L&F's model entirely
options.feedback: Incorrect. They complement each other. L&F explains the appraisal process, and context-specific effectiveness evaluates strategy appropriateness.

toLevel5.stem: Analyse the potential consequences of ignoring context-specific effectiveness when advising someone on coping strategies.

options.text: Advice may be inappropriate for the person's situation, potentially increasing stress if the strategy does not match their demands, resources, or circumstances
options.feedback: Correct. Ignoring context can lead to inappropriate advice that fails to address the actual demands, potentially making the situation worse.

options.text: There are no consequences because all advice about coping is equally helpful
options.feedback: Incorrect. Inappropriate advice can increase stress. Context-specific effectiveness ensures strategies match the person's unique situation.

options.text: The person will always find the right strategy on their own regardless of advice
options.feedback: Incorrect. Without considering context, people may adopt strategies that do not match their situation, potentially increasing stress.

options.text: Ignoring context is actually better because it simplifies the decision-making process
options.feedback: Incorrect. While simpler, ignoring context risks recommending inappropriate strategies that may worsen stress.

toLevel5.stem: How does the concept of context-specific effectiveness protect against oversimplified claims about coping strategies in popular media?

options.text: It reminds us that media claims about 'the best' coping strategy ignore individual differences in demands, resources, and circumstances
options.feedback: Correct. Context-specific effectiveness challenges universal claims by recognising that strategy effectiveness depends on individual circumstances, resources, and demands.

options.text: It does not protect against oversimplified claims because all claims are equally valid
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness provides a framework for critically evaluating oversimplified claims about universally effective strategies.

options.text: Media claims about coping are always accurate so no protection is needed
options.feedback: Incorrect. Media often oversimplifies by promoting one strategy as universally effective. Context-specific effectiveness provides a critical lens.

options.text: Context-specific effectiveness supports media claims about one best strategy
options.feedback: Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness directly challenges the idea of one universally best strategy.

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate whether context-specific effectiveness means that no general guidance about coping strategies can ever be given.

options.text: No — general principles can be taught, but their application must be tailored to specific situations, recognising that effectiveness depends on context
options.feedback: Correct. General principles (like the existence of approach and avoidance strategies) are valuable, but their application must consider the specific demands, resources, and circumstances of each situation.

options.text: Yes — context-specific effectiveness means no general advice is ever useful
options.feedback: Incorrect. General principles about coping are useful as a foundation. Context-specific effectiveness means their application should be tailored.

options.text: Yes — because every situation is so unique that no guidance applies anywhere
options.feedback: Incorrect. While every situation is unique, general principles can still guide strategy selection. The key is applying them to the specific context.

options.text: No — because general guidance overrides context-specific considerations
options.feedback: Incorrect. General guidance is useful but should not override context-specific considerations. Both general principles and specific analysis are important.

toLevel5.stem: Context-specific effectiveness challenges {{blank:1}}-size-fits-all approaches to stress management because different people face different {{blank:2}} with different demands.

distractors.feedback: Incorrect. The phrase is 'one-size-fits-all', referring to a single approach applied universally. Context-specific effectiveness challenges this idea.
Incorrect. The concept challenges 'one-size-fits-all' approaches, not 'no-size-fits-all'. General principles can still be taught.
Incorrect. Context-specific effectiveness relates to different people facing different stressors, not different rewards.
Incorrect. While schedules may be one factor, the broader concept is that different people face different stressors with different demands.
